title: Supreme Court Says Mail Ballots Can Flow Normally for Midterms
summary:
Have you ever waited for a letter that almost didn't arrive? For millions of voters, that's what this year's midterm elections felt like — until Monday night. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump's push to give the U.S. Postal Service a big role in deciding who could receive a mail ballot. The decision means election offices across the country can send out mail ballots as they had planned, without new last-minute rules.

"Now, we can finally move forward and get back to what we do best: conducting our elections without a dark cloud hanging over us," said California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.

The case started with an executive order Trump signed in March. His plan would have required states to use a uniform envelope style for mailed ballots and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn't comply. A whistleblower report warned that millions of mail ballots might never be sent.

About one-third of U.S. voters use mail ballots. In eight states — California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — almost everyone votes by mail. Officials there worried they couldn't adapt in time.

Lower courts had blocked the plan. The Supreme Court refused to let it go forward, saying the administration was "unlikely to succeed on the merits." Three justices — Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh and Clarence Thomas — wanted to let Trump carry out his plan. But the majority sided with the status quo.

"Presidents don't run elections, the people do," said Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read.
why_it_matters: If your family votes by mail, this decision means your ballot should still arrive on time, and it shows that even the president cannot change election rules by himself at the last minute.

It said only California can use mail ballots
It rejected Trump's plan to give the Postal Service a big role in mail ballots

background_read: The Supreme Court (the highest court in the United States, whose decisions no other court can overrule) has the final say on arguments about elections.

President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) signed an executive order in March that tried to change how mail ballots are delivered by the U.S. Postal Service (the government service that brings letters and packages to every address in the country).
Oregon was the first state to run all of its elections by mail, and several other states have since followed its lead, which is why officials there were so worried about last-minute changes.
Article_Structure: WHO: The U.S. Supreme Court, President Donald Trump, the U.S. Postal Service, and state election officials like California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read.
WHAT: The Supreme Court refused to let Trump's plan change how mail ballots are sent, so election offices can send out ballots the way they had planned.
WHERE: Across the United States, especially the eight states where almost everyone votes by mail — California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington.
WHY: The Court doubted the plan would win in court, and officials warned that new rules at the last minute would make it impossible to get ballots to voters in time.

perspectives.description: They are relieved, because they can now print and mail ballots on schedule instead of scrambling to follow new rules.

perspectives.perspective: The Trump administration and the three dissenting justices
perspectives.description: They wanted the Postal Service to check voter lists and envelope styles, arguing that would make mail voting safer.
They point out that courts often end up deciding election fights, and that the real question is how much power a president should have over how voting works.
